title: The Arab Spring: Hope and Its Aftermath

cards.b:
In late 2010 and 2011 protests spread across the Arab world. Dictators fell in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya. Other countries saw long conflicts or new repression. The events became known as the Arab Spring.

The Arab Spring showed how quickly a region can change, and how hard it is to build a stable state after a revolution.

cards.h: A fruit seller in Sidi Bouzid
cards.b:
On 17 December 2010 a young street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid, a town in central Tunisia, after police confiscated his goods. His death sparked protests that spread quickly across the country.

The protests were about jobs, corruption and police abuse. Social media helped spread the images, but the anger came from long-running economic and political grievances.

cards.h: Ben Ali flees, then Tahrir Square
cards.b:
Tunisia's president, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, fled the country on 14 January 2011. In Egypt, huge crowds gathered in Tahrir Square in Cairo. President Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011 after weeks of protest.

Egypt's revolution was a turning point. The square became a symbol of mass protest, and millions of people took part in marches across the country.

cards.h: Marc Lynch on the new Arab politics
cards.b:
Marc Lynch, The Arab Uprising (2012)

Lynch, a political scientist, argues that the uprisings were about dignity, politics and economic justice. He shows how the old regimes had depended on repression and patronage.

His work helps explain both the hope of 2011 and the setbacks that followed.

cards.h: The Arab Spring in key dates
cards.b: The timeline shows how a wave of hope turned quickly into struggle, with different results in each country.

In Libya, protests in February 2011 turned into civil war. NATO air forces supported rebel forces, and Muammar Gaddafi was killed in October 2011. The country then split between rival governments and armed groups for years.

Historians argue about the role of outside intervention. Some say it saved lives. Others say it left Libya without a strong state and helped spread weapons across the region.

cards.h: Was it a social media revolution?
cards.b:
Many accounts describe the Arab Spring as a revolution made by Facebook and Twitter. The phrase is catchy and has been repeated many times.

Historians argue that technology mattered, but the uprisings were rooted in unemployment, food prices, corruption and repression. Social media spread the message faster, but it did not create the grievances. The story of the internet is only one part of the picture.

Protests in Syria began in March 2011, and the government responded with force. The protests became a civil war, with many armed groups, foreign powers and millions of refugees. The war has been one of the most devastating conflicts of the century.

Syria shows how a peaceful protest can turn into a long war, and how regional and global powers can shape its course.

Tunisia remained the most successful case. It adopted a new constitution in 2014 and held competitive elections. In 2015 the Tunisian National Dialogue Quartet, a group of unions and employers, won the Nobel Peace Prize for its role in the transition.

Tunisia's path has also been fragile. Economic problems and political tensions have grown in recent years, and historians debate how durable its democracy will be.

Historians offer several reasons for the setbacks. Old security forces stayed powerful, opposition movements were divided, and outside powers backed rival sides. In some countries the military took back control.

The Arab Spring did not fail in every way. It changed what people expected from their governments, and it showed the limits of authoritarian rule. Its legacy is still being written.

Gulf states and regional powers backed different sides across the region. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates supported counter-revolution in several places, while Qatar and Turkey supported Islamist and rebel groups in others.

The result was a region split by rivalries. This added to the conflicts in Libya, Syria and Yemen, and it made each country's transition harder.

In 2011, while the Arab world rose, India saw its own mass protests. Anna Hazare fasted at Jantar Mantar in Delhi to demand an anti-corruption law. Huge crowds gathered in cities across India, and the movement became one of the largest protests of the decade.

India also had a large stake in the Arab world. Millions of Indians worked in the Gulf, and the Indian government evacuated thousands of its citizens from Libya in 2011 when the fighting began.

Five things to remember
  1. The protests began in Tunisia on 17 December 2010.
  2. Ben Ali left Tunisia in January 2011.
  3. Mubarak resigned in February 2011.
  4. Gaddafi was killed in October 2011.
  5. Tunisia's transition won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize.
Think about it
  • Did the Arab Spring fail, or did it change expectations?
  • How much do social media and economic anger each matter?
